Garbage Collection (GC) tuning in the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is a critical operational discipline required to achieve low latency, predictable throughput, and optimal resource utilization under high-load production environments. By default, ergonomics make reasonable guesses, but enterprise systems demand absolute control over memory sizing and collection behavior. The flag -Xms sets the initial heap size, avoiding costly dynamic heap expansion operations during application startup and early traffic surges. Conversely, -Xmx caps the maximum heap size, preventing the JVM from consuming boundless host memory and triggering Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer executions. Setting -Xms and -Xmx to the same fixed value is a standard production best practice to eliminate heap resizing overhead entirely.

Moving beyond raw sizing, modern enterprise Java relies heavily on advanced collector algorithms like the Garbage-First collector, enabled via -XX:+UseG1GC. G1 breaks the heap into thousands of equal-sized regions, dynamically prioritizing collections on regions containing the highest garbage density (hence Garbage-First). To constrain how long application threads are stopped for collection, engineers use -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis to set a soft target for maximum pause time. The G1 collector dynamically adjusts the size of young and old generations, as well as the number of mixed collection threads, to honor this pause target while attempting to clean up sufficient memory. Mastering these flags requires a deep understanding of card tables, remembered sets (RSet), and parallel marking cycles.

rows: Allocates initial heap memory on startup. Eliminates dynamic resizing pauses when set equal to -Xmx.
Hard ceiling for the JVM heap. Prevents runaway memory consumption and physical host exhaustion.
Enables the region-based Garbage-First collector designed for large heaps with predictable pause times.
Sets a soft real-time target for maximum GC stop-the-world pause duration (default is 200ms for G1).

items: Initial and Maximum Heap Sizing (-Xms, -Xmx): Fixing these values prevents the OS and JVM from negotiating memory pages during peak traffic spikes, eliminating sudden micro-stutters caused by heap resizing cycles.

G1 Collector Mechanics (-XX:+UseG1GC): Unlike traditional generational collectors that require contiguous memory for Eden, Survivor, and Tenured spaces, G1 uses non-contiguous regions. This eliminates fragmentation and allows concurrent marking phases without full heap scans.

Pause Time Target (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis): G1 uses a predictive analytical model based on historical collection times to decide how many regions to collect in a single pause, balancing throughput against latency constraints.

# Production-grade JVM startup arguments for a microservice with a 4GB heap
java \
  -Xms4g \
  -Xmx4g \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
  -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45 \
  -XX:+ParallelRefProcEnabled \
  -Xlog:gc*,gc+phases=debug,safepoint=info:file=/var/log/app/jvm-gc.log:time,uptime,pid:filecount=5,filesize=50M \
  -jar /app/service.jar

A common anti-pattern in production is setting -Xmx to match the total RAM of the container. Always leave headroom for off-heap memory allocations—such as Metaspace, Direct Byte Buffers, thread stacks, and native JNI allocations—or the Linux kernel will ruthlessly terminate your Java process with exit code 137.
